node.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
node.period_rationale: The exchange runs from Bliss (1991–92) to the 2000 reassessments, inside period_3 (c. 1985–2000); its roots (1967, 1969) and the 2009 volume lie outside. groups.json gives period_3, continuing.
node.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Publication dates of the debate texts. 1967 and 1969 are roots, not the start of the debate; 2009 is a later intervention, not its end.

node.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.
node.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in cdn_political_national; Bliss's primary placement is cdn_political_national; this entry keeps his debate row (Q80, user decision 2026-10-12). The replying fields are proposed as cdn_working_class, cdn_women_gender and cdn_regional. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Reid (1987); Buckner (1988). Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).

representative_people.name: Michael Bliss
representative_people.context: Opened the debate: specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country; historians should remember that "their subject, after all, is Canada" (1991–92, abstract).
representative_people.works: "Privatizing the Mind: The Sundering of Canadian History, the Sundering of Canada" (1991–92)

representative_people.name: J. L. Granatstein
representative_people.context: Carried the charge to a public audience: academic historians had abandoned a national past for "overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history" (as summarized by McKillop). Book unread.
representative_people.works: Who Killed Canadian History? (1998; rev. ed. 2007)

representative_people.name: Gregory S. Kealey
representative_people.context: Replied to Bliss in the Journal of Canadian Studies 'Point-Counterpoint' (1992), defending class analysis; the title answers Bliss's directly ("neither privatizing, nor sundering"). Text unread. Not a reply to Granatstein. Primary placement proposed in cdn_working_class.
representative_people.works: "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering" (1992)

representative_people.name: Linda Kealey
representative_people.context: First author of the women's historians' reply to Bliss in the JCS 'Point-Counterpoint' (1992), asking whose "national" history was being lamented. Text unread. Distinct from Gregory Kealey; the citation graph keys this record to "kealey".
representative_people.works: "Teaching Canadian History in the 1990s: Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (1992, with Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag)

representative_people.name: Ruth Roach Pierson
representative_people.context: Co-author of the 1992 reply to Bliss in the JCS 'Point-Counterpoint' (title level). Primary placement proposed in cdn_women_gender.
representative_people.works: "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (1992)

representative_people.name: Joan Sangster
representative_people.context: Co-author of the 1992 reply to Bliss in the JCS 'Point-Counterpoint' (title level). Primary placement proposed in cdn_women_gender.
representative_people.works: "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (1992)

representative_people.name: Veronica Strong-Boag
representative_people.context: Co-author of the 1992 reply to Bliss; her 1994 CHA presidential address answers "neo-conservative laments" by indicting an old history preoccupied with "white male elites" and blind to gender, race and class (abstract); she also reviewed Granatstein's book (1999; unread). Primary placement proposed in cdn_women_gender.
representative_people.works: "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (1992); "Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory" (1994); review of Who Killed Canadian History? (1999)

representative_people.name: A. B. McKillop
representative_people.context: The principal academic reply to Granatstein, in the Canadian Historical Review (80:2, 1999): his narrow national history "can be viewed instead as part of the process of political legitimation", and facts are "inseparable from considerations of value" (abstract).
representative_people.works: "Who Killed Canadian History? A View from the Trenches" (1999)

representative_people.name: Bryan D. Palmer
representative_people.context: A dissident reading of Granatstein in the Canadian Historical Review (80:4, 1999; title level) and a respondent in the 2000 CHR forum; later reviewed Contesting Clio's Craft critically. Primary placement proposed in cdn_working_class.
representative_people.works: "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); review of Contesting Clio's Craft (2010)

representative_people.name: Micheline Dumont
representative_people.context: Reviewed Who Killed Canadian History? in the CHA Bulletin (1999; read in full): his facts on Quebec schooling are 'erronées', his 'réquisitoire est féroce contre les praticiens de l'histoire sociale', and his dismissal of history not aimed at Canadian unity betrays 'visées politiques'. She ties the book to Quebec's national-history debate (Comeau and Dionne 1998; Létourneau). Primary placement in quebec_historiography; also on the cdn_women_gender roster.
representative_people.works: Review of Who Killed Canadian History? (1999)

representative_people.name: Bernard Dionne
representative_people.context: Reviewed Who Killed Canadian History? in RHAF (1998; title level, text unread); co-editor of À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998) in the Quebec debate.
representative_people.works: Review of Who Killed Canadian History? (1998)

representative_people.name: Nadia Fahmy-Eid
representative_people.context: Reviewed Who Killed Canadian History? in the Bulletin d'histoire politique (1999; title level, text unread).
representative_people.works: Review of Who Killed Canadian History? (1999)

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Coined "limited identities" in 1967 (Buckner); in 2000 argued that the debate between limited-identity social history and a renewed "national" approach ignored that identities are contingent and multiple (abstract). Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.
representative_people.works: "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); "'Identities Are Not Like Hats'" (2000)

representative_people.name: J. M. S. Careless
representative_people.context: Popularized "limited identities" of region, culture and class in 1969 (via Buckner's quotations); Reid (1987) reports him also voicing concern about fragmentation in the 1980s.
representative_people.works: "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969)

representative_people.name: John G. Reid
representative_people.context: Reported in 1987 that "concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result" of the new fields of the 1960s and 1970s, from an Atlantic perspective on general syntheses (opening read). Primary placement proposed in cdn_regional.
representative_people.works: "Towards the Elusive Synthesis" (1987)

representative_people.name: Phillip Buckner
representative_people.context: Assessed limited identities from Atlantic Canada before the debate (1988: "premature to abandon") and revisited the concept in 2000, tracing it to Cook and Careless and to the politics of the late 1960s. Primary placement proposed in cdn_political_national.
representative_people.works: "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship" (1988); "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000)

representative_people.name: Jocelyn Létourneau
representative_people.context: Opened the 2000 CHR forum in French: neither a unitarist nor a fragmenting narrative, but a narration of Canada through its dissonant connections, "canadianité" (abstract). His Passer à l'avenir (2000) treats history, memory and identity in Quebec.
representative_people.works: "L'avenir du Canada: par rapport à quelle histoire?" (2000); Passer à l'avenir (2000)

representative_people.name: Doug Owram
representative_people.context: Respondent in the 2000 CHR forum (contribution unread). An anchor of this entry in groups.json; primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.
representative_people.works: Forum response, CHR 81:2 (2000)

representative_people.name: Ian McKay
representative_people.context: Offered the liberal order framework as a way "beyond the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse" (2000, abstract). Primary placement proposed in liberal_order_framework.
representative_people.works: "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000)

representative_people.name: Ken Osborne
representative_people.context: Placed the school-history alarm in a century of recurring "crises" that arose from fears for Canada's future outside the schools (2000, abstract).
representative_people.works: "'Our History Syllabus Has Us Gasping'" (2000)

strands.title: Roots: limited identities
strands.focus: Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969) made region, culture and class the frame; Buckner (1988) judged it premature to abandon; Reid (1987) records the first worries about fragmentation. The debate grows out of this, not out of the 1990s alone.
strands.works: Ramsay Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations," International Journal 22, no. 4 (1967): 659–663.; J. M. S. Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada," Canadian Historical Review 50, no. 1 (1969): 1–10.; Phillip A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship: An Atlantic Provinces Perspective," Journal of Canadian Studies 23, no. 1–2 (1988): 177–198.; John G. Reid, "Towards the Elusive Synthesis: The Atlantic Provinces in Recent General Treatments of Canadian History," Acadiensis 16, no. 2 (1987): 107ff.

strands.title: Phase one, 1991–92: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies
strands.focus: Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (JCS 26:4, 1991–92): specialization had displaced older historians' concern with explaining the country (abstract). A 'Point-Counterpoint' in JCS 27:2 (1992) answered him with 'counter-positions … on the centralist views of Canadian history as articulated by Michael Bliss' (MUSE framing): Gregory Kealey defended class analysis as 'neither privatizing, nor sundering'; Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented (both title level). Strong-Boag's 1994 CHA address answered 'neo-conservative laments' (abstract). These pieces predate Who Killed Canadian History? and are not replies to it.
strands.works: Michael Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind: The Sundering of Canadian History, the Sundering of Canada," Journal of Canadian Studies 26, no. 4 (1991–92): 5–17.; Gregory S. Kealey, "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering," Journal of Canadian Studies 27, no. 2 (1992): 123–129.; Linda Kealey, Ruth Pierson, Joan Sangster and Veronica Strong-Boag, "Teaching Canadian History in the 1990s: Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" Journal of Canadian Studies 27, no. 2 (1992): 129–131.; Veronica Strong-Boag, "Presidential Address: Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association 5, no. 1 (1994): 3–17.

strands.title: Phase two, 1998–99: Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies
strands.focus: Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), which named the debate, took the charge to a public audience (as McKillop summarizes it: academic historians had abandoned a national past for 'overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history'). In the CHR McKillop (80:2, June 1999) argued that Granatstein miscasts the scholar as citizen and that his national history is itself political legitimation; Palmer (80:4, December 1999) offered 'a dissident view' (title level). Strong-Boag reviewed the book in Historical Studies in Education (1999; unread). Francophone historians answered the book too, as reviewers: Dionne in RHAF (1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc in the BHP (1999), Dubuc reading it as a lament for political history as a discipline (first page); and Dumont in the CHA Bulletin (1999, read in full), who corrected its claims about Quebec schooling and called it a fierce indictment of social historians. No francophone reply to Bliss was found.
strands.works: J. L. Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (Toronto: HarperCollins, 1998; rev. ed. Toronto: HarperPerennial, 2007).; A. B. McKillop, "Who Killed Canadian History? A View from the Trenches," Canadian Historical Review 80, no. 2 (1999): 269–300.; Bryan D. Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches: A Dissident View of Granatstein's Meaning," Canadian Historical Review 80, no. 4 (1999): 676–686.; Veronica Strong-Boag, review of Who Killed Canadian History?, Historical Studies in Education 11, no. 2 (1999): 283–285.; Bernard Dionne, review, RHAF 52, no. 2 (1998).; Félix Bouvier, review, BHP 7, no. 2 (1999).; Nadia Fahmy-Eid, review, BHP 7, no. 3 (1999).; Jack Jedwab and Grégory Slogar, review, BHP 7, no. 3 (1999).; Alfred Dubuc, "À propos de : Qui a tué l'histoire du Canada ?", BHP 8, no. 1 (1999).; Micheline Dumont, review, CHA Bulletin 25, no. 1 (1999).

strands.title: Reassessments of 2000
strands.focus: The CHR forum on Létourneau's call for a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions (respondents include Cook, Valverde, Miller, Owram, Tillotson, Palmer, Iacovetta, Mitchinson); Cook on contingent, multiple identities; Buckner revisiting limited identities; McKay's liberal order as an exit from the impasse; Osborne on school history.
strands.works: Jocelyn Létourneau, "L'avenir du Canada: par rapport à quelle histoire?" Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 2 (2000): 229ff., with forum responses by Ramsay Cook, Mariana Valverde, J. R. Miller, Doug Owram, Shirley Tillotson, Bryan D. Palmer, Franca Iacovetta and Wendy Mitchinson (pp. 230–301).; Ramsay Cook, "'Identities Are Not Like Hats'," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 2 (2000), CHR forum.; P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.; Ian McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (2000): 616ff.; Ken Osborne, "'Our History Syllabus Has Us Gasping': History in Canadian Schools — Past, Present, and Future," Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 3 (2000): 403ff.

strands.title: Beyond the impasse
strands.focus: Contesting Clio's Craft (2009) seeks to move past political-versus-social history through transnational and comparative approaches; Palmer's review finds old debates "at times … misrepresented"; Hamilton (2012) finds most Journal of Canadian Studies contributors of 1999–2009 adopted limited identities.
strands.works: Christopher Dummitt and Michael Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft: New Directions and Debates in Canadian History (London: Institute for the Study of the Americas, 2009).; William Trevor Hamilton, "Canada's Story: Canadian Identity and the Journal of Canadian Studies" (2012), TSpace, University of Toronto.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The fragmentation charge against the new social history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Bliss (abstract): twenty-five years of "intense … specialization" replaced older historians' concern for explaining the country. Granatstein, as McKillop summarizes him, accused academic historians of abandoning the national past for "overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history". Cook (2000, abstract) identifies the target as the social history that flowered from limited identities. The critique is from the debate's national side; the replies follow as separate critiques. Scoped to Canadian social history; if cdn_working_class and cdn_women_gender are accepted they carry the specific replies.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Labour historians answer the fragmentation charge
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Two phases. Gregory Kealey answered Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' in the 1992 Journal of Canadian Studies 'Point-Counterpoint', titled "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering"; Palmer's "Of Silences and Trenches: A Dissident View of Granatstein's Meaning" (CHR 80:4, 1999) answers Granatstein's 1998 book. Title and metadata only: neither text was read. PhD context: 22 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the cdn_working_class anchor set (65% vs 22% of all; lift 2.96). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Women's and gender historians answer the lament for national history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Linda Kealey, Ruth Pierson, Joan Sangster and Veronica Strong-Boag, "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (JCS 1992, title), part of the Point-Counterpoint answering Bliss, not Granatstein. Strong-Boag's 1994 address (abstract): "Neo-conservative laments about the state of Canadian history abound"; the old history's "preoccupation with white male elites" and neglect of women and gender, "race" and class show "a restricted vision". She also reviewed Granatstein's book (1999; unread). PhD context: 19 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the cdn_women_gender anchor set (56% vs 25% of all; lift 2.22). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Limited identities and regional history as the debate's ground
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5): Cook coined and Careless popularized "limited identities" of region, culture and class. Cook (2000, abstract): the hypothesis "played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed 'national' approach". Reid (1987) and Buckner (1988) show the fragmentation worry and the Atlantic defence of limited identities before Bliss. Contribution as background and defence; regional historians are not presented as one side. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the cdn_regional anchor set (41% vs 15% of all; lift 2.77). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: National-political history as one side of the debate
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Contesting Clio's Craft (description) names "the political vs. social history debates that have dominated the field since the 1970s". McKay (2000) calls it the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse". Bliss and Granatstein are political and business historians (see cdn_political_national). Comparison: not every political historian took Granatstein's side. PhD context: 24 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the cdn_political_national anchor set (71% vs 19% of all; lift 3.8). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Lament for an older national history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Bliss (abstract) contrasts specialization with "older Canadian historians' concern for explaining the nature of the country" while warning against "nationalist mythologizers"; Buckner (2000) describes that older consensus around the nation-state. Comparison: the debate invokes the tradition; it does not restore the staple or Laurentian theses. PhD context: 20 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the cdn_national_tradition anchor set (59% vs 13% of all; lift 4.43). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Parallel debates over national narrative in English Canada and Quebec
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Dumont's review of Who Killed Canadian History? (CHA Bulletin 1999, read in full) joins the two debates: she corrects Granatstein's claims about Quebec schooling, calls his book a fierce indictment of social historians with 'visées politiques', and cites Ferretti's chapter in Comeau and Dionne, eds., À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998), and Létourneau's student surveys. Dionne, who reviewed the book in RHAF (1998; title level), co-edited that volume. Létourneau (CHR 2000, abstract) proposes a narration of Canada that is neither unitarist nor fragmenting. Comparison: concurrent, separate debates linked through a few people, not texts; no checked Quebec-debate text cites Bliss or Granatstein (research Q81), and only 4 strict 2009–2026 PhDs cite texts from both. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the quebec_historiography anchor set (41% vs 16% of all; lift 2.63). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over what historians owe facts and publics
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: McKillop (1999, abstract) answers Granatstein that "event-driven facts are inseparable from considerations of value and therefore from the realm of the interpretive". Comparison only: the Canadian debate was about national history and specialization, not postmodernism; no checked text links it to Jenkins, Evans or Appleby, Hunt and Jacob.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: groups.json lists revival. No checked debate text refers to Stone's narrative revival or the quantification debate. Not proposed.
Granatstein addressed a public audience and Osborne wrote on school history, but no checked text ties the debate to the atlas public-history field; history education has no atlas entry.
Highest overlap of the group engagement set (lift 4.6) is driven by shared anchors (Owram, Palmer), not debate texts. No textual link checked.
Strong-Boag's title speaks of "the politics of Canadian memory"; the abstract concerns historians' vision, not memory studies. Not proposed.
Proposed in the liberal_order_framework draft as lof_rel_09 (McKay 2000 abstract plus Ajzenstat 2009); not duplicated here. McKay 2000 stays in this roster and strand.

open_questions: The brief asks for links to the social, gender and labour groups. I propose a critique from the debate to the atlas `social` entry and replies (critiques) from cdn_working_class and cdn_women_gender. If those proposed groups are not accepted, should the replies retarget to the atlas `labourhistory` and `women`/`gender` entries?
Several replies are title-level only (G. Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). Should someone read them before the edges are accepted?
Bliss's primary placement: here (groups.json) or cdn_political_national (most of his citations come from business history)?
Is Létourneau's 2000 forum the right francophone presence, or should the Quebec curriculum and national-narrative debates of the 2000s be a separate comparison?

The debate texts are cited by only 34 strict 2009–2026 PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. Is the entry justified mainly for teaching rather than uptake? (The user decided it is its own entry; this is a note for the description's register.)
Person ids: other drafters may choose different ids for shared people (e.g. ramsay_cook, j_m_s_careless, phillip_buckner). Each roster row carries candidates_csv_name so ids can be reconciled.

question_resolutions.summary: Moot: cdn_working_class and cdn_women_gender were accepted, so the replies keep their proposed endpoints.

Split into a 1991–92 strand (Bliss and the JCS Point-Counterpoint replies; Strong-Boag 1994) and a 1998–99 strand (Granatstein and the CHR replies by McKillop and Palmer; Strong-Boag's review, newly verified in Crossref). Palmer's venue recorded as CHR 80:4; the 1992 pieces are described as replies to Bliss, nowhere as replies to Who Killed.

Bliss's primary placement not moved (same as Q73); his row keeps proposed_primary_placement who_killed_debate with a placement_status note. Applied after the user decision 2026-10-12: michael_bliss primary placement is now cdn_political_national; roster rows kept.

Research applied: Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999, full text) added as a critic; Dionne and Fahmy-Eid as title-level critics (needs_review); Bouvier, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc as sources only. Scope note revised (francophones answered Granatstein, not Bliss; Quebec's debate ran separately). cdng_wk_rel_07 re-grounded on Dumont; Fecteau 1999 removed. Claude's review (2026-10-12): each reading is now attributed to the reviewer whose text was checked (Dubuc first page; Dumont full text); Dionne's review is unread and is not characterised.
Description and scope note now present the entry as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding, not current practice, with the 2.6% (falling to 2.0%) uptake in the scope note.
Ids were reconciled in consolidation; nothing to change.
